Hi Oliver —

Thanks again for the call earlier. Attached is a short ask so our engineering team can finalize the Dedicated sizing proposal: a small sample of peak QPS/seq-length distribution (CSV), and a baseline SLO target. Quick clarifications we need before we lock SKUs: 

1) Typical request shape: percent of requests with context > 8k tokens vs > 64k tokens? You mentioned two long-context features — ballpark splits help.
2) Tail latency SLO at p95 and p99 (ms) and whether you can accept a low-cost degraded path for non-interactive batch requests.
3) Expected sustained QPS during 9–5 (PST) and expected burst multiplier.

High-level guidance we plan to evaluate (so you're aware of tradeoffs):
- L4 is very economical for short-context / low-memory models (embedding, scoring) and for high QPS low-latency needs.
- A100 is a balanced option for medium-long contexts with good memory and steady throughput.
- H100 unlocks best long-context throughput and quantization flexibility but at higher per-hour cost and denotes concentrating fewer larger slots.

We'll run a quick slotting simulation once we have the CSV (sample attached). If it's helpful, we can propose a 3-tier allocation: L4 pool for baseline low-cost traffic, A100 for mid-weight generator requests, and a smaller H100 pool for long-context stateful workloads and pre-warm caching.

Next step: if you can drop the requested CSV or confirm the three bullets above, we will return a firm capacity spreadsheet and recommended fallthrough policy by Tuesday.

Thanks,

Folks —

I ran the sample through our slotting simulator and sketched three candidate fleet configurations (summary below). Quoting Oliver inline where relevant.

Key inputs from sample: sustained 45 QPS business hours; burst 3x; 8% >8k tokens; 0.6% >64k tokens. SLOs: p95 1200ms, p99 up to 2.5s.

Candidate A (cost-minimal / L4-heavy)
- L4 pool: covers up to 70% of requests (short-context scoring / embeddings); scaled to 35 QPS sustained, burstable to 90 QPS.
- A100 pool: small pool for mid-length gen requests (handles ~25% of mixed load).
- H100: minimal (1–2 GPUs) reserved purely for >64k token stateful runs; these are isolated and run with high memory slots.
- Notes: Lowest monthly cost; risk is higher contention when mid-length gen latency climbs under burst. Works if customer can accept occasional fallbacks for interactive long-context during bursts.

Candidate B (balanced / recommended starter)
- L4 pool: sized for 30 QPS baseline; auto-scale to handle up to 2x bursts for short requests.
- A100 pool: primary workhorse — sized to cover 60% of gen load during business hours with steady latency.
- H100 pool: 4 GPUs to cover concurrent >8k sequences and provide KV-cache friendly slots for long sessions.
- Tradeoff: ~18% higher cost than A but much better p95/p99 adherence under the stated bursts. Good for customers prioritizing UX and predictable latencies.

Candidate C (latency-first / H100-weighted)
- H100 pool: larger footprint (8 GPUs) to absorb long-context and provide high single-req throughput; A100 only used as overflow; L4 for tiny scorable traffic.
- Cost: highest but tightest tail latency. Preferred when many users rely on 64k+ sessions interactively.

Operational recommendations (applies across candidates)
- Prefix/KV caching: pre-warm most frequent sessions on H100 nodes (saves ~30% compute for repeated long-context flows).
- Quantization profile: use FP16 on A100; H100 can run mixed precision for models that need >24GB memory; consider int8 (where compatible) on L4 for embeddings and scoring.
- Autoscale policy: target headroom of 20% sustained with burst buffer and rapid scale for L4 (sub-30s), slower scale for H100 (2–5 minutes due to model load times).
- Fallback path: route non-critical long-context to queued batch run with lower priority and different SLA (p95 5s) during extreme bursts.

I'll attach a proposed_capacity_breakdown.xlsx with slot assumptions and estimated monthly cost deltas for each candidate. Suggest we present Candidate B to the customer first and keep Candidate A as a lower-cost opt-in.
